## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pārājika 2 (*Adinnādāna*, "The training rule on stealing") is the Vinaya treatise expounding the second rule of defeat (*pārājika*) for Buddhist monks [SuttaCentral]. According to the rule, any monk who with intent to steal takes what has not been given (*adinnam theyyasaṅkhātaṃ ādiyeyya*) from a village or a wilderness, to an extent for which civil authorities would arrest, imprison, flog, or banish a thief, is defeated and expelled from the saṅgha [Banerjee 1979; Collins 2001; SuttaCentral]. The text's origin story relates that the monk Dhaniya appropriated timber belonging to the king; the casuistry specifies that the initial instigator of the rule (*ādikammika*) was free from guilt, an exemption explained by Buddhaghosa in the *Samantapāsādikā* as applying directly to Dhaniya [Rosen 1959]. The vibhaṅga provides precise definitions of legal terminology, explaining what constitutes intentional theft as well as providing explicit definitions of "village" (*gāma*) and "wilderness" (*arañña*) [Bhikkhu Sujato 2009; Collins 2001].

Parallels for this rule exist in every surviving early Buddhist Vinaya tradition, encompassing both the Bhikkhu and Bhikkhunī Pātimokkhas and Vibhaṅgas of the Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Dharmaguptaka, and Lokottaravāda schools across Sanskrit, Chinese, and Tibetan recensions, as well as the Pāli Parivāra and the *Senāsanakkhandhaka* (Kd 16) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus detects extensive internal textual reuse with other Pārājika rules (particularly Pj 1, Pj 3, and Pj 4), the Saṅghādisesa chapter, Khandhaka treatises, and Vinaya commentaries including the *Pārājikakaṇḍa-aṭṭhakathā*, *Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā*, and *Vinayavinicchaya-ṭīkā* [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns the text with Sanskrit *Prātimokṣasūtra* fragments and Tibetan Vinaya translations, including the Tibetan *Vinayavibhaṅga* (D0003) and *Vinaya-uttaragrantha* (D0007) [DharmaNexus].
